purpose: Sarilumab is used to treat moderate to severe rheumatoid arthritis in adults when other medications have not worked well enough. It helps reduce joint pain, swelling, and stiffness. It may also slow down joint damage over time.
how_it_works: Your immune system makes a protein called IL-6 that causes inflammation and joint damage in rheumatoid arthritis. Sarilumab works by blocking the place where IL-6 attaches in your body, like putting a cap over a lock so the key cannot get in. By blocking IL-6, it helps calm down the overactive immune response that is hurting your joints.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include redness, pain, or itching at the injection site, upper respiratory infections like a cold or sore throat, urinary tract infections, and a runny nose. You may also notice that your cholesterol levels go up, so your doctor will check blood work regularly.
warnings: Because sarilumab lowers your immune system's activity, you are at a higher risk of getting serious infections, including tuberculosis (TB), so your doctor will test you for TB before starting treatment. Do not use this medication if you have an active infection. It can also cause low white blood cell counts, low platelet counts, and elevated liver enzymes, which is why regular blood tests are important. Avoid live vaccines while taking this medicine. Tell your doctor about all medications you take, as some drug interactions can occur.
typical_dosing: Sarilumab is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous) once every two weeks. The usual dose is 200 mg, but your doctor may start you at 150 mg if needed. It comes in a pre-filled syringe or auto-injector pen that you can learn to use at home after proper training.
